name: Kotlin
title: Kotlin: a modern language for the JVM and Android
intro: Kotlin was made by JetBrains, the company behind IntelliJ IDEA, and released in 2016. It runs on the Java virtual machine and can use any Java library, but it needs far less typing than Java: no semicolons, types that are worked out for you, and one-line data classes. In 2019 Google made it the preferred language for Android apps, and it is now used for servers and desktop programs too. Its best-known feature is null safety: the compiler knows which values may be missing and won't let you forget to check. Every example here is a whole file and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, install the Kotlin compiler, save the example as Main.kt, and type kotlinc Main.kt -include-runtime -d main.jar and then java -jar main.jar. Or paste it into the Kotlin Playground at play.kotlinlang.org.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.summary: main, println, val and var, string templates.

sections.p: A Kotlin program starts in a function called main. Functions are declared with fun, and they don't have to live inside a class. println prints a value and ends the line; print prints without ending it. Lines don't need semicolons.

val makes a name that can't be given a new value, and var one that can. Use val unless you need to change it; most Kotlin code is mostly val. The type comes after a colon, but usually you leave it out and Kotlin works it out from the value: val nuts = 7 is an Int.
Inside a string, $name puts in the value of a variable, and ${...} puts in the value of any expression. This replaces most of the + joining other languages need.
sections.code:
fun main() {
    val name = "Hazel"
    val nuts = 7
    println("$name has $nuts nuts")
    println("Next week: ${nuts * 2}")
    println("Name length: ${name.length}")
}
sections.out:
Hazel has 7 nuts
Next week: 14
Name length: 5

sections.p: Int holds whole numbers and Double numbers with a fractional part. Dividing two Ints drops the remainder, which % gives you. A Double always prints with a decimal point, even when it is whole. Kotlin never converts between number types by itself: call toDouble() or toInt().
sections.code:
fun main() {
    val nuts = 17
    val squirrels = 5
    println(nuts / squirrels)
    println(nuts % squirrels)
    println(nuts.toDouble() / squirrels)
    val weight = 6.0
    println(weight)
    println(weight.toInt() + 1)
}

practice.why: $acorns and $tree are replaced by their values, and acorns is 6 after += 2.
Int divided by Int drops the remainder. With a Double on one side the answer is a Double.

practice.q: What happens when you give a val a new value?
options: The program stops when it reaches that line
practice.why: A val can be set only once. The mistake is caught before the program runs.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.summary: if as an expression, when, ranges and for.

sections.p: if works as in most languages, but in Kotlin it is also an expression: it gives back a value, so you can put it straight into a val. That replaces the ? : operator that other languages have.
when picks the first branch that matches. A branch can list several values, test a range with in, or be any condition. else catches everything left. Like if, when gives back a value.

1..5 is a range from 1 to 5, both ends included. for walks through a range or a list. until leaves out the last number, downTo counts backwards, and step jumps by more than one. while loops as long as its condition holds.

practice.why: 1..4 includes both ends: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.
when without a value tests each condition in turn and takes the first true one. 7 < 5 is false, 7 < 10 is true.

practice.q: How many times does  for (i in 0 until 4)  run?
practice.why: until leaves out the end, so i takes 0, 1, 2 and 3.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Parameters, default and named arguments, one-line functions, lambdas.

sections.p: Parameters need their types, and the return type goes after the brackets. A parameter can have a default value, so callers can leave it out. Callers can also name arguments, which makes a call with several numbers easier to read and lets them come in any order.

When a function just returns one expression, write = and the expression instead of braces and return. Kotlin works out the return type. A function that returns nothing useful returns Unit, which you don't write.

A lambda is a function without a name, written in braces: { n: Int -> n * 3 }. You can keep one in a val and pass it to other functions. When a lambda has one parameter you can leave it out and call it it. When a lambda is the last argument, it goes after the brackets.

practice.why: count defaults to 1. Named arguments can come in any order.
The lambda after the brackets is f, and it stands for its one parameter, 5.

sections.p: In Kotlin a plain String can never be null. When a value may be missing, add a question mark to the type: String?. The compiler then won't let you use it as if it were there. Inside an if (x != null) check, Kotlin knows it is there and lets you use it normally; this is called a smart cast.

?. is the safe call: name?.length gives the length, or null if name is null. ?:, the Elvis operator, gives a fallback when the left side is null. Together they replace most null checks. !! says "I'm sure this isn't null" and crashes if you're wrong, so use it rarely.

Many library functions return a nullable value when there may be no answer. toIntOrNull() turns text into a number, or null if the text isn't one. firstOrNull finds the first matching item, or null. ?.let { ... } runs a block only when the value is there.
sections.out:
42
null
Found beech
no huge tree

practice.why: a?.length is null, so ?: gives 0. b?.length is 4. 0 + 4 = 4.
"x" isn't a number, so toIntOrNull gives null and ?: turns it into 0: 3 + 0 + 5.

practice.q: What is the difference between String and String? ?
practice.why: Kotlin keeps null out of plain types, so a missing value can only appear where the type says it may.

lessons.title: Lists and maps
lessons.summary: listOf and mutableListOf, maps, filter, map and friends.

sections.p: listOf makes a list that can't be changed. mutableListOf makes one you can add to and remove from. Read an item with list[0]; the first item is number 0. Printing a list shows its items in square brackets.
sections.code:
fun main() {
    val trees = listOf("oak", "ash", "beech")
    println(trees)
    println(trees[1])
    println(trees.size)
    val stash = mutableListOf(3, 5)
    stash.add(8)
    stash.remove(3)
    println(stash)
    println("ash" in trees)
}

sections.p: A map stores values under keys. "oak" to 4 makes a key and value pair. Looking up a key that isn't there gives null, so the result type is nullable and ?: is handy. In a for loop, (key, value) takes each pair apart.

Lists come with many functions that take a lambda. filter keeps the items that pass a test, map turns each item into something else, and sum, count, maxOrNull and sortedBy do what their names say. Chaining them often replaces a whole loop.
sections.code:
fun main() {
    val nuts = listOf(4, 11, 7, 2, 9)
    println(nuts.filter { it > 5 })
    println(nuts.map { it * 10 })
    println(nuts.filter { it % 2 == 1 }.sum())
    println(nuts.count { it < 5 })
    println(nuts.maxOrNull())
    val trees = listOf("beech", "oak", "chestnut")
    println(trees.sortedBy { it.length })
    println(trees.joinToString(" / ") { it.uppercase() })
}

practice.why: filter keeps 2, 4 and 6, and map squares each of them.
Looking up a missing key gives null rather than an error.

options: It doesn't compile: listOf makes a read-only list
practice.answer: It doesn't compile: listOf makes a read-only list
practice.why: A List has no add. Use mutableListOf when you need to change it.

lessons.title: Classes and data classes
lessons.summary: Constructors, properties, methods and data classes.

sections.p: A class's main constructor goes right after its name. Writing val or var in front of a parameter makes it a property in one step. Create an object by calling the class like a function; Kotlin has no new. private hides a property from code outside the class.

Classes that mainly hold data are so common that Kotlin has data class. It writes the boring parts for you: a readable toString, == that compares the contents, and copy to make a changed copy. Data classes can also be taken apart into separate vals.
sections.code:
data class Nut(val kind: String, val grams: Int)

fun main() {
    val a = Nut("hazel", 3)
    val b = Nut("hazel", 3)
    println(a)
    println(a == b)
    val big = a.copy(grams = 5)
    println(big)
    val (kind, grams) = big
    println("$kind weighs $grams g")
}
sections.out:
Nut(kind=hazel, grams=3)
true
Nut(kind=hazel, grams=5)
hazel weighs 5 g

sections.p: An interface lists what a class must provide, and override marks each function that provides it. Kotlin classes are closed by default: another class can extend one only if it is marked open. A List of the interface type can hold any class that implements it.
sections.out:
Hazel says chitter
Sage says hoo

practice.code:
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val p = Point(1, 2)
    val q = p.copy(y = 5)
    println(q)
    println(p == Point(1, 2))
}
practice.why: copy changes only y. A data class compares its contents with ==, so an equal Point counts as equal.
Each object has its own count. a has ticked twice and b once.

lessons.title: Sealed classes and when
lessons.summary: A fixed set of cases, is checks, and when that covers them all.

sections.p: A sealed class or interface has a fixed list of subclasses, all in the same file. That lets when check that every case is handled: no else is needed, and adding a new case makes the compiler point at every when that misses it. Inside a branch, is has already smart-cast the value, so its own properties can be used.

Sealed types are a good way to return either a value or a reason it failed, instead of throwing an exception. The caller has to look at which one it got. An object is a class with exactly one instance, useful for a case with no data.
sections.out:
found 12
nothing in the ash
never heard of it

sections.p: An enum class is a type with a fixed list of named values. Each value knows its name and its position, ordinal, and entries lists them all. Like sealed types, a when over an enum can cover every value without else.
sections.out:
0 SPRING: eat
1 SUMMER: eat
2 AUTUMN: bury nuts
3 WINTER: dig them up

practice.why: Pet is sealed, so the compiler knows Dog and Fish are the only cases and no else is needed.

practice.q: Why does a when over a sealed type not need an else branch?
options: The compiler knows every possible subclass
else is never needed in Kotlin
when picks the first branch anyway
practice.answer: The compiler knows every possible subclass
practice.why: All subclasses of a sealed type are known when it is compiled, so the compiler can check that each one is handled.

lessons.title: Extensions and generics
lessons.summary: Adding functions to existing types, type parameters, and scope functions.

sections.p: An extension function adds a function to a type you didn't write, even String or Int. Inside it, this is the value it was called on. It doesn't really change the type; it's a normal function that is called with a dot.
sections.code:
fun String.shout() = uppercase() + "!"
fun Int.isBig() = this > 100

fun main() {
    println("hello squirrel".shout())
    println(250.isBig())
    println(7.isBig())
}

sections.p: A generic function has a type parameter in angle brackets, <T>, standing for whatever type the caller uses. List<String> and Map<String, Int> are generic types you have already met. Kotlin works out T from the arguments, and the result keeps the right type.

let, apply and also run a block with a value. let calls it it and gives back the block's result, which suits nullable values. apply calls it this and gives back the value itself, which suits setting up an object. also does a side job, like printing, and passes the value on.

practice.why: squared is an extension on Int, so 3.squared() is 9 and 4.squared() is 16.
T is String in the first call and Int in the second, so sum works: 1 + 2 + 1.

lessons.title: Errors and Result
lessons.summary: try and catch, require, Result and runCatching.

sections.p: When something goes wrong, Kotlin throws an exception and the nearest matching catch handles it. Code in finally runs either way. require checks a condition and throws an IllegalArgumentException with your message when it fails, which is the usual way to reject bad arguments.
sections.out:
left: 7
checked 3
refused: asked for 12, only 10 left
checked 12
bad input: want must be non-negative
checked -1

sections.p: Result<T> is either a success holding a value or a failure holding an exception. Callers look at it with getOrNull, getOrElse or getOrDefault, so a failure can't be forgotten the way an uncaught exception can. Result.success and Result.failure build the two cases.

runCatching { ... } runs a block and wraps either its value or the exception it threw in a Result. map transforms a successful value and leaves a failure alone; recover turns a failure into a value. isSuccess and isFailure ask which case you have.

practice.why: require throws before b prints; the catch runs, then finally.
The failure becomes 0, so 2 + 0 + 5 = 7.

practice.q: What does runCatching { ... } return when the block throws?
practice.why: runCatching catches the throw and wraps it, so the caller can decide what to do.

lessons.title: Grouping and folding
lessons.summary: groupBy, fold, flatMap, associateWith and friends.

sections.p: groupBy builds a map from a key to the list of items that share it. Chaining mapValues turns each list into a total. groupingBy { ... }.eachCount() counts how many times each key appears without building the lists first.

fold walks the list with a running total, starting from the value you give it: each step gets the total so far and the next item. flatMap turns each item into a list and concatenates the results, so one item can become several.
sections.code:
fun main() {
    val finds = listOf(3, 5, 2, 4, 1)
    println(finds.fold(0) { acc, n -> acc + n })
    println(finds.fold(1) { acc, n -> acc * n })
    println(listOf(1, 2, 3).flatMap { n -> listOf(n, n * 10) })
    println((1..5).map { it * it }.joinToString("-"))
}

sections.p: associateWith makes a map whose keys are the list items and whose values come from a lambda. associate builds each key–value pair itself. On a map, filterValues keeps the entries whose values pass a test.

practice.why: eachCount counts how many times each key appears; oak appears twice.
fold starts at 1 and multiplies by each item: 1×2×3×4 = 24.
flatMap concatenates the small lists into one list.

lessons.title: Project: a nut inventory
lessons.summary: Data classes, sealed events and a Result-style apply together.

sections.p: An inventory is built by replaying a list of events. Each event is one case of a sealed interface, so when must handle every kind. Taking more nuts than you have is a failure returned as a sealed result, not thrown. A gift that asks for more walnuts than you have is skipped and reported; the rest become a sorted table.
sections.out:
skipped: cannot gift 5 walnut: only 3
acorn      5
hazelnut   4
walnut     3
gifts to: Pip

sections.p: Add a Traded event that swaps one nut for another and see the compiler point at the unhandled case, keep a history of every stock along the way, or switch the sealed ApplyResult for the built-in Result type.

practice.q: Why does apply return ApplyResult instead of throwing?
options: So a bad event can be skipped and reported without stopping the whole replay
Kotlin cannot throw inside a when
practice.answer: So a bad event can be skipped and reported without stopping the whole replay
practice.why: Returning an error value keeps the loop in charge, the same idea as Result.
entries() gives both enums in order, name.lowercase() makes the keys readable, and acorn is then increased.

options: A new Stock with one count changed, leaving the old Stock alone
The same Stock, mutated in place
Only the new count as an Int
null when the nut is missing
practice.answer: A new Stock with one count changed, leaving the old Stock alone
practice.why: counts + (n to v) builds a new map; data classes are usually treated as values.
